questions.q: What specifically does RLAIF change compared to the RLHF pipeline from Chapter 7?
options: It replaces PPO with a completely different RL algorithm
Only the source of the preference label — an AI judge model generates it instead of a human annotator — while reward model training, evaluation, and PPO/DPO stay identical
It removes the need for a reward model entirely
It changes the Bradley-Terry objective into a different loss function
questions.explain: RLAIF swaps out exactly one component, the preference label source; every downstream step in the pipeline is unchanged from Chapter 7.

questions.q: What does an AI judge model receive as input to produce a preference label?
options: Only the final reward model score, with no text at all
The original prompt, both candidate responses, and a rubric describing what to prefer, then it picks a winner
A randomly generated numeric score with no prompt or responses
The PPO training logs from a previous run
questions.explain: The judge prompt in this lesson shows the prompt, both responses, and a rubric (helpful, accurate, harmless) being given to the judge model, which then picks A or B.

questions.q: What shape of data does the AI judge's output produce, and why does that matter for the rest of the pipeline?
options: A single scalar reward value, incompatible with reward model training
The same (prompt, chosen, rejected) shape that human-labeled preference pairs produce, meaning the rest of the pipeline cannot distinguish AI-labeled from human-labeled data
A full fine-tuned model checkpoint
A ranked list of ten candidate responses
questions.explain: Because the AI judge's output is converted into the same chosen/rejected format used in Chapter 6, downstream reward model training and RL fine-tuning work without any modification.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does RLAIF exist — what problem is it solving?
options: It exists purely as an academic exercise with no practical motivation
The cost, speed, and scale limitations of human preference labeling at the volume frontier models need, plus inconsistency across human annotators
Because reward models cannot be trained on human-labeled data at all
Because PPO cannot run without AI-generated labels
questions.explain: Human labeling is expensive, slow, and inconsistent across annotators at the scale needed; an AI judge can label continuously and apply the same criteria consistently.

questions.q: What is the key tradeoff this lesson flags for using an AI judge instead of human annotators?
options: There is no tradeoff at all — AI judges are strictly superior in every respect
An AI judge inherits whatever blind spots that judge model itself has, in exchange for consistency, speed, and lower cost
AI judges can never produce preference labels in the required format
AI judges always produce worse reward models than any human-labeled alternative
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes that the gain in consistency and scale comes at the cost of inheriting the judge model's own blind spots — a tradeoff explored further in lesson 51.
